title: Cloudflare Cuts 100 TB of Memory from 1.1.1.1 DNS Cache
gist: Cloudflare redesigned the in-memory representation of its Big Pineapple DNS cache in Rust, cutting per-entry memory footprint 56%, freeing about 100 TB of fleet-wide working-set memory, increasing cache insertion throughput 43%, and reducing lookup latency 19%, illustrating how low-level data-structure engineering can produce outsized infrastructure cost savings at hyperscale.

insights.claim: Cloudflare redesigned the in-memory representation of its 1.1.1.1 resolver's DNS cache, reducing the benchmarked per-entry footprint by 56% and freeing roughly 100 TB of working-set memory across its fleet, while increasing cache insertion throughput by 43% and reducing lookup latency by 19%.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Concrete, sizable evidence that data-structure-level optimization at hyperscale can free massive capacity (100 TB) without new hardware spend — a template ROI case for infrastructure engineering investment.
insights.locator: Cloudflare has redesigned the in-memory representation

insights.claim: Cloudflare's Big Pineapple DNS platform stores more than 250 billion DNS cache entries at any given time.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Scale context: at 250B+ entries, even single-digit byte-level savings per entry compound into terabytes, explaining why Cloudflare invested engineering effort here.
insights.locator: Big Pineapple stores more than 250 billion DNS cache entries

insights.claim: The optimization involved five successive changes to cache representation in Rust: replacing Vec and String with Box<[T]> and Box<str> for data fixed after insertion (saving 64 bytes per entry, over 15 TB fleetwide), combining answer/authority/additional records into one list with compact offsets, packing Booleans into bitflags, and omitting owner names matching the queried domain by reconstructing them from the cache key.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A concrete, reusable list of Rust memory-optimization techniques (boxed slices over Vec, bitflag packing, key-derived field elision) applicable to any high-cardinality in-memory cache system.
insights.locator: The work involved five successive changes

insights.claim: Cloudflare's largest engineering challenge involved Rust enums: initially boxing larger variants to save space, but the separate allocations added overhead and reduced memory locality, so the final design instead stores record data in a contiguous byte buffer using DNS wire format, removing enum and per-record allocation overhead while improving locality.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A non-obvious lesson for Rust systems engineers: naive enum-boxing to save memory can backfire on cache locality at scale; wire-format contiguous buffers outperformed a 'more idiomatic' boxed-enum approach.
insights.locator: The largest challenge involved Rust enums

insights.claim: One Reddit commenter noted that many of these memory-optimization tricks (such as avoiding boxed enum variants) only pay off at Cloudflare's request volume; at smaller scale, the extra indirection from boxing variants can actually hurt cache locality more than it helps.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A caveat against blindly copying hyperscaler optimization patterns: these techniques are scale-dependent and may not benefit (or could even hurt) smaller systems.
insights.quote: A lot of these memory tricks only pay off once you're at Cloudflare's request volume; at a smaller scale the extra indirection from boxing variants can actually hurt cache locality more than it helps.
insights.locator: One Reddit commenter summarized the tradeoff

insights.claim: The optimization was rolled out across production between May 18 and July 6, 2026; at p99, resident memory per instance fell from 9.3 GB to 5.3 GB, while p90 memory declined from 6.5 GB to 3.8 GB.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Roughly 43% p99 and 42% p90 reduction in per-instance memory footprint gives a directly verifiable production benchmark, not just a lab claim.
insights.locator: The optimization was rolled out across production

insights.claim: Benchmarks showed the per-entry cache footprint falling from 953 to 420 bytes and allocations from 1.1 KB to 461 bytes; Cloudflare plans to use the roughly 100 TB of freed fleet-wide working-set memory to increase cache capacity without increasing overall memory consumption.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Freed capacity will be reinvested into larger cache sizes rather than cost reduction alone, implying Cloudflare expects further DNS cache hit-rate/performance gains from this work rather than treating it purely as a cost play.
insights.locator: Benchmarks showed the per-entry footprint falling

insights.claim: Cloudflare's approach differs from other recursive DNS resolvers: Unbound maintains separate message, RRset, key, and negative caches with configurable cache sizes and slab settings, while PowerDNS Recursor uses multiple cache types including packet and record caches, whereas Cloudflare instead focuses on reducing representation and allocation overhead within individual cache entries.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Identifies a distinct architectural philosophy (per-entry representation optimization vs. multi-cache-type segmentation) that differentiates Cloudflare's DNS infrastructure from open-source alternatives like Unbound and PowerDNS — relevant for anyone benchmarking or selecting resolver architectures.
